4D Rotations and Chirality
In four-dimensional space, rotations are significantly more complex than in 3D. While you are correct that there are basic directions of rotation for any given plane (CW and CCW), 4D rotations are often classified as isoclinic rotations. These come in two distinct types: left-isoclinic and right-isoclinic.
This means that while a simple rotation in a single plane has two directions, a "double rotation" (where two orthogonal planes rotate simultaneously) can be decomposed into a left-handed component and a right-handed component. Therefore, the concept of two chiralities remains a fundamental symmetry in 4D, but it applies to the way the two independent planes of rotation interact rather than just the direction within a single plane.
